prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology and active form of glucagon-like peptide-1 that enabled incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us ranked B042 first, which tells us little about merit by itself, so the case needs to stand on its own. It does: the arc from the incretin effect, through proglucagon processing and the demonstration that GLP-1(7-36) amide is the active insulinotropic peptide, to receptor biology and long-acting agonists is among the most complete bench-to-bedside chains in recent medicine. The effects on glycaemia, weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes are demonstrated in large randomized trials and in broad clinical use over more than a decade. A prize built on Holst, Drucker and Mojsov keeps the citation on discovery of the physiology and the active peptide, which is where the Nobel tradition places credit, and it fits within the three-person limit without needing a second part.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The credited list spans physiological discovery, peptide identification and drug development, and any three names omit someone whose contribution was substantial: Knudsen on the pharmaceutical side and Habener and others, who are not on the list, on the identification side. Mojsov's priority relative to the Habener group is contested, and I am relying on recollection of the historical record. There is also a real risk that a prize centred on discovery will be read as ignoring the drug-development step that actually changed patients' lives.

responses.point: El-Manira proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, treating the long-acting analogues as a necessary part of a complete arc from physiology to therapy.
responses.response: I take the point that the story is incomplete without the analogues, and I do not dismiss Knudsen's role in liraglutide and semaglutide. But the committee's most defensible unit is the discovery of the hormone's physiology and active form, and a citation resting on that can acknowledge therapy as its consequence without crediting the drug company's engineering. Choosing Knudsen over Mojsov also removes the one person who identified and synthesised the active peptide, which is a discovery rather than development. I would reconsider if colleagues argue that the prize should explicitly be about therapy, in which case Knudsen replaces Mojsov or Holst and the citation changes.

responses.point: Sandberg placed B033 (unfolded protein response, Walter and Mori) second and described the credit as a clean, compact two-person configuration, while ranking B049 CAR-T with only June and Sadelain as the cleanest version.
responses.response: I agree that the Walter and Mori attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist, and that is its strength: the mechanism is original and well understood. My reservation, which I hold as a qualification rather than a disagreement, is that its clinical consequences are still emerging, so it is a very strong candidate for a later year or for pairing, not a reason to displace B042 now. On B049 I would resist trimming Rosenberg too quickly. Adoptive cell transfer and the first gene-modified T-cell trials are part of why CAR-T works clinically, so a two-person prize risks being a narrower story than the field actually is.

responses.point: The chair, while ranking B042 first, noted that the credited list spans physiological discovery, peptide identification and drug development, and that a three-person prize centred on the biology omits Knudsen and perhaps others.
responses.response: I agree that this is the central problem and do not think it can be resolved from the supplied record. My view is that the discovery framing is the more defensible, and that it can be stated honestly in the citation. I would however welcome the chair's guidance on whether a prize split into two parts, with GLP-1 biology as one part and a separate achievement as the other, is realistic under the three-person limit, since B042 alone already uses all three names. I do not see a pairing that improves the attribution problem.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius saw Holst and Drucker as the clearest scientific anchors for GLP-1, with Mojsov's contribution real but more difficult to credit, and ranked B033 second and B049 third.
responses.response: I agree Holst and Drucker are the anchors, and I would not put Mojsov in if the record showed her contribution to be derivative. I keep her because the identification and chemical synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) form is the specific step that made the hormone's therapeutic action intelligible, and I regard that as discovery. Where I differ is that I would not call this settled: if the committee can verify that the Habener group's work is equal or prior, the three-name set must be reopened, and I would rather say so now than assume it.

uncertainties: Priority between Mojsov and the Habener group for identification of the active GLP-1 peptide, and whether the record supports crediting Mojsov over Knudsen.
Whether the committee frames the prize as discovery of physiology or as therapy development, which determines whether Knudsen is included.
Whether B033 or B049 would be better paired or held for a later year, given that attribution in B049 spreads across Eshhar, Rosenberg, June and Sadelain.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. I co-authored the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper and have co-authors in common with Rickard Sandberg, but none of the shortlisted names are my documented collaborators, and I do not infer further ties.
